title: Earth and Space Science: Earth's Structure, Plate Tectonics, the Rock Cycle, Weather and Climate, Hazards, and the Solar System; Full Review
objectives: Students will describe Earth's layers and explain how Earth's four systems interact.
Students will match each type of plate boundary to the landforms and hazards it produces and solve plate-motion rate problems.
Students will explain how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks form in the rock cycle.
Students will distinguish weather from climate and explain the greenhouse effect and the cause of the seasons.
Students will interpret solar system and natural hazard data and apply science practices in a cumulative review of life, physical, and earth and space science.
teach:
Week 10 Science: Earth and Space — Earth's Structure, Plate Tectonics, the Rock Cycle, Weather and Climate, Natural Hazards, and the Solar System; Cumulative Review

Objectives

  • Describe Earth's layers and Earth's four interacting systems (geosphere, hydrosphere, atmosphere, biosphere).
  • Explain plate tectonics and match each type of plate boundary to the landforms and hazards it produces.
  • Trace the rock cycle and identify how igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks form.
  • Distinguish weather from climate, explain the greenhouse effect, and explain the cause of the seasons.
  • Describe the solar system and universe, and solve GED-style earth and space problems that use rates, data, and comparisons, while reviewing life science, physical science, and science practices.

Materials

  • Whiteboard or shared screen; markers in two colors.
  • Printed or on-screen copy of this week's Student Lesson, Study Notes, and Post Lesson review checklist.
  • A ball (for Earth) and a lamp or flashlight (for the Sun) to model the seasons and Moon phases.
  • This week's 12 practice items (course page) for independent practice.

60-Minute Timing Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5Weather or climate? Sort four statements; one quick review question from earlier weeks.
Direct instruction20Earth's layers and systems, plate tectonics, rock cycle, weather and climate, hazards, solar system; Worked Examples 1–4.
Guided practice15Coastal city vs. inland city temperature data, with a physical science connection.
Independent practice15Practice items 1–12 on the course page (mixed earth/space and full-course review).
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding; walk through the full-course review checklist and test-day strategy in the Post Lesson.

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Write these statements on the board. Ask: "Which describe weather (conditions right now or over a few days) and which describe climate (the long-term average pattern)?"

  1. It snowed four inches last night.
  2. This region averages 50 inches of rain per year.
  3. Summers in this valley are usually hot and dry.
  4. A cold front will bring storms on Thursday.

Review question: "A student tests whether the amount of salt in water changes how fast ice melts. What is the dependent variable?"

Answers: 1 and 4 are weather (short-term conditions). 2 and 3 are climate (long-term averages and patterns, usually over 30 years or more). A handy phrase: climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.

Review: The dependent variable is how fast the ice melts (for example, the time until it is fully melted). The amount of salt is the independent variable.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes) — Talking Points

1. Earth's layers. Draw a circle with four rings. From the outside in: the crust (thin, solid rock; we live on it), the mantle (the thickest layer; hot, mostly solid rock that flows very slowly over long periods), the outer core (liquid iron and nickel; its motion produces Earth's magnetic field), and the inner core (solid iron and nickel; it is the hottest layer, but enormous pressure keeps it solid). Temperature and pressure both increase with depth. Stress that the mantle is not a sea of liquid rock; this is a common misconception.

2. Earth's systems. Earth works as four connected systems: the geosphere (rock and soil), the hydrosphere (all water, including ice), the atmosphere (air), and the biosphere (living things). GED questions often ask how a change in one affects another. Example: a volcanic eruption (geosphere) sends ash into the atmosphere, which can cool the climate and reduce crop growth (biosphere).

3. Plate tectonics. The crust and the rigid top of the mantle are broken into large pieces called tectonic plates. Heat from Earth's interior drives slow convection currents in the mantle, and the plates move a few centimeters per year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Most earthquakes, volcanoes, and mountain ranges are found along plate boundaries. Write the three boundary types on the board:

BoundaryMotionWhat forms
DivergentPlates move apartMid-ocean ridges, rift valleys, new crust from rising magma
ConvergentPlates push togetherOcean plate under continent: deep trench, volcanoes, strong earthquakes. Continent with continent: tall mountains such as the Himalayas.
TransformPlates slide past each otherEarthquakes along faults; few or no volcanoes

Evidence for plate movement: matching fossils and rock types on continents now separated by oceans, the puzzle-like fit of South America and Africa, sea floor that is youngest at mid-ocean ridges, and the pattern of earthquakes and volcanoes along plate edges.

4. The rock cycle. Rocks are constantly recycled. Igneous rock forms when magma (underground) or lava (on the surface) cools and hardens. Weathering breaks rock into sediment, erosion carries it away by water, wind, or ice, and deposition drops it in layers. Layers that are pressed and cemented become sedimentary rock, the kind most likely to contain fossils. Any rock exposed to great heat and pressure, without melting, becomes metamorphic rock. Any rock that melts becomes magma again. Emphasize that the cycle has no fixed order; any rock type can become any other.

5. Weather and climate. The Sun drives both. Uneven heating of Earth's surface causes winds and ocean currents, which move heat from the equator toward the poles. The water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection) moves water between the hydrosphere and atmosphere. The greenhouse effect is natural: gases such as carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor absorb heat radiating from Earth's surface and keep the planet warm enough for life. Adding more of these gases, mainly by burning fossil fuels, traps more heat and raises global average temperatures. Large bodies of water heat and cool slowly, so coastal places have milder climates than inland places at the same latitude.

6. Natural hazards. Earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis, landslides, hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, and droughts. Scientists cannot prevent them, but they reduce harm through monitoring, warning systems, building codes, and land-use planning. Earthquake magnitude is measured on a scale where each whole number increase means about 10 times more ground shaking (wave amplitude) and about 32 times more energy released.

7. The solar system and universe. The Sun is a medium-sized star at the center of our solar system. Its gravity holds eight planets in orbit: four small, rocky inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) and four large, gaseous outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune). Planets farther from the Sun take longer to complete an orbit. Earth's 23.5° tilt causes the seasons: the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets more direct sunlight and longer days. Earth's rotation causes day and night; its revolution around the Sun takes one year. The Moon's phases happen because we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth (about 29.5 days). Our solar system is one small part of the Milky Way galaxy, one of billions of galaxies. Distances are measured in light-years (the distance light travels in one year). Evidence such as galaxies moving away from one another supports the Big Bang theory: the universe began expanding about 13.8 billion years ago. Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.

Worked Example 1 — Plate motion rate. A plate moves about 5 cm per year. How far will it move in 1 million years? Give the answer in kilometers.

Solution: distance = rate × time
5 cm/year × 1,000,000 years = 5,000,000 cm
5,000,000 cm ÷ 100 = 50,000 m
50,000 m ÷ 1,000 = 50 km.
Teaching point: tiny yearly motion adds up to huge distances over geologic time.

Worked Example 2 — Comparing earthquake magnitudes. Earthquake A has magnitude 6.0. Earthquake B has magnitude 4.0. How many times greater is the ground shaking of A? About how many times more energy does A release?

Solution: Difference in magnitude = 6.0 − 4.0 = 2.
Shaking: 10 × 10 = 102 = 100 times greater.
Energy: 32 × 32 = 1,024, or about 1,000 times more energy.
Teaching point: a magnitude 6 is not "one and a half times" a magnitude 4. Each step multiplies.

Worked Example 3 — Weather vs. climate with data. The July high temperature at a weather station for five years was 91°F, 93°F, 90°F, 94°F, and 92°F. On one July day this year, the high was 99°F. Which number describes climate, and what is it?

Solution: Climate is the long-term average.
Sum: 91 + 93 + 90 + 94 + 92 = 460
Mean: 460 ÷ 5 = 92°F.
The 99°F day is weather: one day's conditions. (In real climate studies, scientists use 30 or more years of data.)

Worked Example 4 — Cumulative review: energy in a food chain. After a wildfire, grasses regrow and store 10,000 kJ of energy. Rabbits eat the grass, and foxes eat the rabbits. About how much of the energy reaches the foxes?

Solution: Use the 10% rule: about 10% of the energy passes to each next level.
Grass to rabbits: 10,000 × 0.10 = 1,000 kJ
Rabbits to foxes: 1,000 × 0.10 = 100 kJ.
Teaching point: natural hazards (geosphere) affect ecosystems (biosphere); GED questions often link the two.

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Display this table. Work through the questions together; call on different students for each step.

CityMean January temperature (°C)Mean July temperature (°C)
Coastal City (on the ocean)1022
Inland City (same latitude, 800 km from the ocean)−430
  1. What is the yearly temperature range (July minus January) for each city?
  2. Which city has the milder climate?
  3. Use what you learned in physical science to explain the difference.
  4. Does this table describe weather or climate? How do you know?

1. Coastal: 22 − 10 = 12°C. Inland: 30 − (−4) = 30 + 4 = 34°C. (Watch for students who write 26 by ignoring the negative sign.)

2. Coastal City; its range is much smaller.

3. Water has a high specific heat: it absorbs and releases heat slowly. The ocean stays cooler in summer and warmer in winter than land, so it keeps nearby air temperatures moderate.

4. Climate. The values are long-term monthly means, not one day's readings.

Checks for Understanding

  • "Which layer is liquid?" Expected: the outer core.
  • "What type of boundary forms the Himalayas?" Expected: convergent, continent with continent.
  • "How does a sedimentary rock become a metamorphic rock?" Expected: heat and pressure change it without melting it.
  • "Why is it summer in the Northern Hemisphere in July?" Expected: the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so sunlight is more direct and days are longer.
  • "How much more shaking is a magnitude 7 than a magnitude 5?" Expected: 10 × 10 = 100 times.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

"Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun." Correction: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, during Northern Hemisphere winter. Use the ball and lamp to show tilt: the same lamp gives direct light to one hemisphere and slanted light to the other.

Mixing up weather and climate. Correction: ask, "Is this one day or week, or a long-term average?" One cold winter does not disprove a warming climate trend.

Treating the magnitude scale as ordinary counting. Correction: each step is a multiplication by 10 (shaking). Have students write the multiplication out: 10 × 10 × 10 for a difference of 3.

"Moon phases are caused by Earth's shadow." Correction: Earth's shadow on the Moon is a lunar eclipse, which is rare. Phases come from our changing view of the Moon's sunlit half.

Thinking the rock cycle runs in one direction. Correction: draw the cycle with arrows in many directions; any rock can be weathered, buried, heated, or melted.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a blank Earth cross-section and a blank boundary table to fill in during instruction. Pair "weather or climate" statements with a two-column sort. For rate problems, give the frame "distance = rate × time" and a units chart (100 cm = 1 m; 1,000 m = 1 km).

Stretch: Ask students to explain why the youngest sea floor is at mid-ocean ridges and the oldest is near trenches. Or have them compare two planets from a data table and predict, with reasons, which has the longer year and why the hottest planet (Venus) is not the closest to the Sun (its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere creates an extreme greenhouse effect).

How This Shows Up on the GED

Earth and space science is about one-fifth of the GED Science test, so expect several questions, nearly always tied to a stimulus: a diagram described in text, a data table of planets or earthquakes, a climate graph, or a short reading about a hazard. Expect wording like:

  • "Based on the table, which type of plate boundary most likely…?"
  • "Which statement describes climate rather than weather?"
  • "Which conclusion about the eruption is best supported by the graph?"
  • "How many years would it take the plate to move…?"
  • "Which pattern in the data supports the scientist's hypothesis?"

Formats include multiple choice, drop-down menus completing an explanation, drag-and-drop sorting (rock types, boundary types), fill-in calculations (rates, means), and select-two items from planet or weather data. Because this is the final week, remind students that the remaining 80% of the test is life science and physical science, and every content area is tested through the same science practices: reading data, identifying variables, and choosing the best-supported conclusion.

Wrap-up (5 minutes)

Run the checks for understanding above. Then open the Post Lesson together: walk through the full-course Science review checklist, have each student circle the two topics they feel least sure about, and read the test-day strategy aloud. Preview this week's Practice GED.
student:
Earth and Space Science, Plus Your Final Science Review

About one-fifth of the GED Science test covers Earth and space. The questions almost always give you a table, graph, or short reading, so you do not need to memorize every fact. You need the big ideas below and the same data skills you have practiced all course.

1. Earth's layers and systems

From the outside in, Earth has four layers:

  • Crust: thin, solid rock. We live on it.
  • Mantle: the thickest layer. Hot, mostly solid rock that flows very slowly.
  • Outer core: liquid iron and nickel.
  • Inner core: solid iron and nickel. Hottest of all, but kept solid by pressure.

Earth also works as four connected systems: the geosphere (rock), hydrosphere (water), atmosphere (air), and biosphere (life). A change in one affects the others. For example, heavy rain (hydrosphere) can trigger a landslide (geosphere) that destroys a forest habitat (biosphere).

2. Plate tectonics

Earth's outer shell is broken into huge tectonic plates that move a few centimeters a year, pushed by slow heat currents in the mantle. Where plates meet, things happen:

BoundaryPlates…Results
Divergentmove apartNew crust, mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys
Convergentpush togetherTrenches, volcanoes, mountains, strong earthquakes
Transformslide past each otherEarthquakes along faults

Worked Example 1. The Atlantic Ocean widens about 2.5 cm per year. How much wider will it be in 100 years?

distance = rate × time = 2.5 cm/year × 100 years = 250 cm.
250 cm ÷ 100 = 2.5 meters.

3. The rock cycle

  • Igneous rock forms when melted rock (magma underground, lava on the surface) cools and hardens.
  • Sedimentary rock forms when bits of rock, sand, mud, or shells settle in layers and are pressed and cemented together. Fossils are usually found here.
  • Metamorphic rock forms when any rock is changed by heat and pressure without melting.

Weathering breaks rock down; erosion carries the pieces away. The cycle has no fixed order. Any rock type can become any other type.

4. Weather, climate, and the seasons

Weather is the condition of the air over hours or days. Climate is the average pattern over many years (usually 30 or more). Climate is what you expect; weather is what you get.

The Sun powers weather. Uneven heating creates winds and ocean currents, and the water cycle moves water through evaporation, condensation, and precipitation. The greenhouse effect happens when gases such as carbon dioxide and methane trap heat near Earth's surface. Some greenhouse effect keeps Earth livable; adding more of these gases, mostly by burning fossil fuels, raises global temperatures.

Seasons are caused by Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun. When your half of Earth tilts toward the Sun, sunlight hits more directly and days are longer, so it is summer.

Worked Example 2. A town recorded yearly rainfall of 12, 9, 14, and 13 inches over four years. What is the mean? Is it weather or climate?

Sum: 12 + 9 + 14 + 13 = 48. Mean: 48 ÷ 4 = 12 inches. A long-term average describes climate (a real climate average would use many more years).

5. Natural hazards

Earthquakes, volcanoes, tsunamis, landslides, hurricanes, tornadoes, floods, and droughts are natural hazards. People reduce damage with warning systems, stronger buildings, and smart planning. Earthquake magnitude grows fast: each whole number up means about 10 times more shaking and about 32 times more energy.

Worked Example 3. How much more shaking does a magnitude 7 earthquake produce than a magnitude 5?

Difference: 7 − 5 = 2 steps. Shaking: 10 × 10 = 100 times more. (Energy: 32 × 32 ≈ 1,000 times more.)

6. The solar system and universe

  • The Sun is a star. Its gravity keeps eight planets in orbit.
  • Inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars) are small and rocky. Outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune) are huge and made mostly of gas.
  • Planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit it. Earth's year is 365 days.
  • Earth's rotation (spinning, once a day) causes day and night. Its revolution (orbit, once a year) plus its tilt causes the seasons.
  • The Moon's phases happen because we see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits Earth about every 29.5 days.
  • Our solar system is in the Milky Way galaxy, one of billions of galaxies. A light-year is the distance light travels in one year. The universe began expanding in the Big Bang about 13.8 billion years ago.

Strategy: When a question gives you a planet or earthquake table, look for a pattern first ("as distance goes up, orbit time goes up"), then check for the one row that breaks the pattern. GED questions love the exception, such as Venus being hotter than Mercury.

Try It

1. Lava from a volcano cools quickly and hardens on the surface. What type of rock forms?

Show answer

Igneous rock. Any rock that forms when melted rock cools and hardens is igneous.

2. A plate moves 4 cm per year. How many years will it take to move 2 meters?

Show answer

2 meters = 200 cm. Time = distance ÷ rate = 200 ÷ 4 = 50 years.

3. How many times more shaking does a magnitude 8 earthquake produce than a magnitude 5?

Show answer

Difference: 8 − 5 = 3 steps. 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times.

4. True or false: The Moon's phases are caused by Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.

Show answer

False. Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. Earth's shadow on the Moon causes a lunar eclipse, which is rare.

5. Review (physical science): A car travels 150 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?

Show answer

speed = distance ÷ time = 150 km ÷ 2 h = 75 km/h.
post:
Post Lesson: Earth and Space, and Your Full Science Review

Summary of Key Points

  • Earth's layers: crust, mantle (mostly solid, flows slowly), liquid outer core, solid inner core.
  • Plates move a few centimeters a year. Divergent = apart, convergent = together, transform = sliding past. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur at plate boundaries.
  • Rock cycle: igneous (cooled melted rock), sedimentary (pressed layers; fossils), metamorphic (heat and pressure, no melting).
  • Weather is short-term; climate is the long-term average. Earth's tilt causes the seasons. Greenhouse gases trap heat.
  • Each step up in earthquake magnitude means about 10 times more shaking.
  • The Sun's gravity holds the planets in orbit; farther planets have longer years.

Exit Ticket

1. What type of plate boundary forms a deep ocean trench?

Show answer

A convergent boundary where an ocean plate sinks beneath another plate.

2. Weather or climate: "Thunderstorms are expected tonight."

Show answer

Weather. It describes short-term conditions.

3. Why is it colder in the Northern Hemisphere in January?

Show answer

The Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun, so sunlight is less direct and days are shorter.

4. Name two renewable energy resources.

Show answer

Any two of: solar, wind, hydroelectric (moving water), geothermal, biomass.

5. Review: A rock sample has a mass of 40 g and a volume of 8 cm3. What is its density?

Show answer

density = mass ÷ volume = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 g/cm3.

Reflection

  • Which science topic from the whole course do you feel most confident about? Which one needs one more review?
  • Think of a natural hazard that could affect your area. What could your household do to prepare?
  • How have the science practices (variables, data, conclusions) helped you on topics you had never studied before?

Full-Course Science Review Checklist

Check off each item you can explain in your own words. Reread the matching week for any you cannot.

AreaI can…
Science practices (Weeks 1–2)Identify independent, dependent, and controlled variables and the control group; judge a fair test; read tables and graphs; find mean, median, mode, and range; find a simple probability; choose the best-supported conclusion.
Cells (Week 3)Name key organelles and their jobs; compare photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
Human body (Week 4)Describe major body systems, homeostasis, nutrition, and how diseases spread.
Genetics (Week 5)Use a Punnett square; tell dominant from recessive and genotype from phenotype.

Chemistry (Week 7)Read the periodic table; balance mass in a reaction; tell physical from chemical changes; use density = mass ÷ volume.

This Week's Study Plan (20–40 minutes a day)

DayTask
Day 1Reread the Student Lesson and redo the five Try It problems without looking. (25 min)
Day 2Complete practice items 1–12. For each miss, write one sentence explaining the correct answer. (35 min)
Day 3Work through the review checklist. Reread the Study Notes for your two weakest weeks. (30–40 min)
Day 4Take this week's Practice GED under timed conditions (about 90 minutes; may be split over two days).
Day 5Review every Practice GED question you missed and sort the misses by area. Redo one earlier week's practice items in your weakest area. (30–40 min)
Day 6Light review only: vocabulary and formulas. Rest well before test day. (20 min)

Test-Day Strategy for GED Science

  • Read the question before the stimulus. Know what you are hunting for, then read the table, graph, or passage with that goal.
  • Pace yourself. You have about 90 minutes. Check the clock every 10 questions. If a question takes more than about 3 minutes, choose your best answer, flag it, and come back if time allows.
  • Use the data, not just memory. Most answers are in the stimulus. If an answer choice says something the data never measured, it is probably wrong.
  • Label experiments fast. Jot C (changed), M (measured), S (same) for any experiment before answering.
  • Use the on-screen calculator for means, rates, and percents, and check that your answer has the right units.
  • Answer every question. An unanswered question cannot earn points, so eliminate what you can and make your best choice.

vocab.example: Plate movement explains why earthquakes cluster along certain coastlines.

vocab.def: The thick layer of hot, mostly solid rock between the crust and the core; it flows very slowly.
vocab.example: Heat currents in the mantle help move tectonic plates.

vocab.def: A place where two plates move apart and new crust forms.
A place where two plates push together, forming trenches, volcanoes, or mountains.
vocab.example: The collision that built the Himalayas.

vocab.def: A place where two plates slide past each other, causing earthquakes.
vocab.example: A long fault where the ground shifts sideways.

vocab.def: The ongoing process by which rocks change from one type (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic) to another.
vocab.example: Granite weathers into sand, which becomes sandstone.

vocab.def: The movement of weathered rock and soil by water, wind, ice, or gravity.
vocab.example: A river carries mud downstream after a storm.

vocab.def: The condition of the atmosphere at a place over hours or days.
The average weather pattern of a place over many years, usually 30 or more.
vocab.example: A desert climate with hot summers and little rain.

vocab.def: The warming of Earth's surface when gases in the atmosphere trap heat.
vocab.example: Carbon dioxide from burning fuel adds to the greenhouse effect.

vocab.example: A magnitude 6 shakes about 10 times more than a magnitude 5.

vocab.def: A natural event that can harm people or property.
The force of attraction between objects with mass; it keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
vocab.example: The Sun's gravity holds Earth in its yearly orbit.

vocab.def: The distance light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers; used to measure distances to stars.
vocab.example: A star 10 light-years away is seen by light that left it 10 years ago.

notes:
Study Notes: Earth and Space + Science Review

Earth's Layers (outside in)

Crust (thin, solid) → Mantle (thickest, mostly solid, flows slowly) → Outer core (liquid iron/nickel) → Inner core (solid, hottest)

Plate Boundaries

  • Divergent (apart): ridges, rift valleys, new crust
  • Convergent (together): trenches, volcanoes, mountains
  • Transform (slide past): earthquakes, faults

Rock Cycle

  • Igneous: magma/lava cools
  • Sedimentary: layers pressed and cemented; fossils
  • Metamorphic: heat + pressure, no melting

Weather, Climate, Seasons

  • Weather = short-term. Climate = long-term average (30+ years).
  • Seasons = Earth's 23.5° tilt, not distance.
  • Greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapor) trap heat.
  • Water heats and cools slowly: coasts are milder.

Space

  • Sun = star; gravity holds 8 planets in orbit.
  • Inner = rocky; outer = gas giants. Farther = longer year.
  • Rotation = day/night. Revolution = 1 year.
  • Moon phases = our view of its lit half (29.5 days).
  • Light-year = distance light travels in 1 year.

Earthquake magnitude: +1 = 10× shaking, about 32× energy. +2 = 100× shaking.

FormulaUse
mean = sum ÷ countAverages, trials, climate data
speed (rate) = distance ÷ timeMotion, plate movement, seismic waves
density = mass ÷ volumeMatter, rocks, floating and sinking
force = mass × accelerationNewton's second law
work = force × distanceMachines and energy
Punnett square: 4 boxes, each 25%Probability of a trait
Food chain: about 10% of energy passes onEcosystems

Watch out: weather ≠ climate. Summer is not caused by being closer to the Sun. Conclusions must stay inside the data.

stimuli.title: Plate Boundaries Around the World
stimuli.html:
Earth's outer shell is made of large tectonic plates that move slowly over the mantle. The table below summarizes four well-studied plate boundaries.

LocationHow the plates moveFeatures observed
Mid-Atlantic RidgeTwo plates move apartUnderwater mountain ridge; new sea floor forms from rising magma; mostly shallow earthquakes
Himalaya MountainsTwo continental plates collideWorld's tallest mountains; frequent earthquakes; few volcanoes
West coast of South AmericaOcean plate sinks beneath a continental plateDeep ocean trench offshore; chain of volcanoes inland; strong earthquakes
A long fault in western North AmericaTwo plates slide past each otherFrequent earthquakes; no volcanoes

Measurements show that the North American and Eurasian plates are moving apart along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge at an average rate of about 2.5 centimeters per year.

options: Outer core
Inner core
Mantle

items.hint: One of the two core layers is solid because of extreme pressure; the other is liquid.
items.explain:
The outer core is liquid iron and nickel. Its flowing metal produces Earth's magnetic field.

The inner core is made of the same metals and is even hotter, but the enormous pressure at Earth's center keeps it solid. The mantle is mostly solid rock that flows very slowly, and the crust is solid rock.

Tomorrow's high temperature is expected to be 95°F.
Strong winds are forecast for this weekend.
items.hint: Climate describes a long-term average; weather describes hours or days.
items.explain:
An average yearly rainfall describes the long-term pattern of a place, which is climate.

The other three statements describe conditions over a single afternoon, a single day, or a weekend. Those are short-term conditions, so they describe weather.

items.prompt: Sort each description into the type of rock it forms.
choices: Lava from a volcano cools and hardens on the surface.
Layers of sand are buried, pressed, and cemented together.
Limestone deep underground is changed by heat and pressure without melting.
Magma cools slowly far beneath the surface.
Shells and mud settle on the sea floor and harden over time.
Shale is squeezed by colliding plates and becomes slate.
items.hint: Melted rock cooling = igneous. Layers pressed together = sedimentary. Heat and pressure without melting = metamorphic.
items.explain:
Igneous: lava cooling on the surface and magma cooling underground. Both start as melted rock.

Sedimentary: sand layers and shells and mud. Both are pieces that settle in layers and are pressed and cemented.

Metamorphic: limestone changed by heat and pressure, and shale squeezed into slate. Both are existing rocks changed without melting. If the rock had melted, it would become magma and then igneous rock.

items.prompt: Scientists study a newly mapped boundary where an ocean plate is sinking beneath a continental plate. Based on the table, which set of features would they most likely find there?
options: A deep ocean trench, a chain of volcanoes, and strong earthquakes
Very tall mountains, frequent earthquakes, and few volcanoes
An underwater ridge where new sea floor is forming
Frequent earthquakes along a fault, with no volcanoes
items.hint: Find the row in the table with the same plate motion.
items.explain:
The west coast of South America is the row where an ocean plate sinks beneath a continental plate. Its features are a deep trench, a chain of volcanoes, and strong earthquakes, so a boundary with the same motion would most likely have the same features.

Tall mountains with few volcanoes match two continental plates colliding (the Himalayas). A ridge with new sea floor matches plates moving apart. Earthquakes with no volcanoes match plates sliding past each other.

items.prompt: At the rate given in the passage, about how many years will it take for the North American and Eurasian plates to move 1 meter farther apart?
items.hint: Convert 1 meter to centimeters first. Then divide distance by rate.
items.explain:
Step 1: Convert units. 1 m = 100 cm.

Step 2: time = distance ÷ rate = 100 cm ÷ 2.5 cm per year = 40 years.

A common error is dividing 1 by 2.5 without converting meters to centimeters, which gives 0.4.

items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?
options: Global temperature fell after the eruption, dropped most about one year later, and returned to the earlier average within about four years.
The eruption caused a permanent drop in global average temperature.
Global average temperature rose by 0.4°C in the year after the eruption.
The eruption had no measurable effect on global average temperature.
items.hint: Look at the sign of each value and at what happens by the last year in the table.
items.explain:
The changes are 0.0 in the eruption year, then −0.4, −0.3, −0.1, and back to 0.0 four years after. The largest drop (−0.4°C) came one year after the eruption, and the temperature returned to the earlier average by year 4.

The drop was not permanent (it returned to 0.0). The value −0.4 is a decrease, not a rise. And a 0.4°C drop is a clear, measurable effect.

items.prompt:
Complete the explanation of the data.

The high haze of tiny droplets {{0}} part of the incoming sunlight back into space. As a result, less energy reached Earth's surface, and global average temperature {{1}} for a few years.

options: reflected
trapped
created
decreased
increased
stayed the same

items.hint: The data show cooling. What must the haze have done with sunlight to cause cooling?
items.explain:
The table shows global temperature decreased after the eruption. Cooling means less of the Sun's energy reached the surface, so the haze must have reflected some sunlight back to space.

"Trapped" describes greenhouse gases, which hold heat in and cause warming, the opposite of what the data show. The haze does not "create" sunlight.

items.prompt: In pea plants, the allele for purple flowers (P) is dominant over the allele for white flowers (p). Two plants with the genotype Pp are crossed. What is the probability that an offspring plant will have white flowers?
items.hint: Draw a 2-by-2 Punnett square. White flowers need two recessive alleles.
items.explain:
Punnett square for Pp × Pp: the four boxes are PP, Pp, Pp, pp.

Only pp has two recessive alleles, so only 1 of 4 boxes shows white flowers: 1 ÷ 4 = 25%.

75% is the probability of purple flowers (PP, Pp, Pp), a common mix-up. 50% is the probability of the Pp genotype.

items.prompt: Which two statements are supported by the data in the table? Select two answers.
options: Planets farther from the Sun take longer to orbit the Sun.
A planet's mean temperature always decreases as its distance from the Sun increases.
Venus has a higher mean surface temperature than Mercury, even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.
Mars takes less than one Earth year to orbit the Sun.
Jupiter's orbit takes about 5 times as long as Earth's orbit.
items.hint: Check each statement against every row. One counterexample is enough to make an "always" statement false.
items.explain:
Supported: Orbit times increase steadily as distance increases (0.24, 0.62, 1.00, 1.88, 11.86, 29.46 years). Venus (464°C) is hotter than Mercury (167°C) even though Venus is farther from the Sun.

Not supported: Temperature does not always decrease with distance; Venus breaks the pattern. Mars takes 1.88 Earth years, which is more than one. Jupiter's orbit takes 11.86 years, about 12 times Earth's, not 5 times. (The number 5 is close to Jupiter's distance, 5.20 AU, which is a different column.)

items.prompt: Earth is about 3% closer to the Sun in early January than in early July. Yet the Northern Hemisphere has winter in January and summer in July. Which statement best explains why the Northern Hemisphere is warmer in July?
options: In July, the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, so it receives more direct sunlight and has longer days.
In July, Earth is closer to the Sun than at any other time of year.
The Sun gives off more energy in July than it does in January.
Earth spins faster in July, so each place faces the Sun for more hours.
items.hint: The question already tells you that distance cannot be the reason.
items.explain:
Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. In July, the Northern Hemisphere tilts toward the Sun. Sunlight strikes it more directly (concentrating energy on a smaller area) and days are longer, so it warms up.

The prompt states Earth is actually closer to the Sun in January, so distance cannot explain July warmth. The Sun's output does not swing between seasons, and Earth's rotation speed does not change with the seasons.

items.prompt: Which choice correctly names the independent variable and states a conclusion supported by the data?
options: Independent variable: tray angle. Conclusion: in this test, steeper slopes lost more soil.
Independent variable: mass of soil washed off. Conclusion: in this test, steeper slopes lost more soil.
Independent variable: tray angle. Conclusion: soil loss doubled each time the angle increased by 10°.
Independent variable: tray angle. Conclusion: slope angle is the only cause of soil erosion.
items.hint: First decide what the student changed on purpose. Then test each conclusion against the actual numbers.
items.explain:
The student changed the tray angle on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The mass of soil washed off is what she measured (the dependent variable).

Soil loss rose at every step (42, 95, 160, 231 g), so steeper slopes lost more soil in this test.

It did not double each time: 42 × 2 = 84 (actual 95), 95 × 2 = 190 (actual 160), 160 × 2 = 320 (actual 231). And the experiment tested only one factor, so it cannot show that slope is the only cause of erosion; rainfall amount, plant cover, and soil type also matter.

items.prompt: An earthquake sends out two kinds of waves at the same moment. P-waves travel through rock at about 6 km/s, and S-waves travel at about 3.5 km/s. A seismic station is 210 km from the earthquake. About how many seconds after the P-waves arrive will the S-waves arrive?
options: 25 seconds
35 seconds
60 seconds
95 seconds
items.hint: Find the travel time of each wave with time = distance ÷ speed, then subtract.
items.explain:
P-wave time: 210 km ÷ 6 km/s = 35 s.

S-wave time: 210 km ÷ 3.5 km/s = 60 s.

Difference: 60 − 35 = 25 seconds.

35 s and 60 s are the separate travel times, not the gap between them. 95 s comes from adding the two times instead of subtracting.
